books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835)

stimulus.text: “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I readily discovered the prodigious influence which this primary fact exercises on the whole course of society, by giving a certain direction to public opinion, and a certain tenor to the laws. . . . The more I advanced in the study of American society, the more I perceived that the equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.” — Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Volume 1 (1835).
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835), Introduction. Verbatim quotation (Reeve translation), verified against the Bill of Rights Institute excerpts. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: A historian could best use this passage to support which claim about the United States in the 1830s?

options.text: Visitors saw American democracy as a way of life beyond voting
Americans had achieved full equality among all people by the 1830s
options.misconception: Tocqueville describes a tendency, and slavery and women's exclusion show its limits.

options.text: Tocqueville believed American democracy was bound to fail
options.misconception: He admired much of what he saw and studied why democracy worked here; this passage praises, not condemns.

options.text: Equality in America came from the Constitution alone
options.misconception: Tocqueville calls equality a fact of society that shapes laws, not a gift of the laws.

rationales.A: Tocqueville says equality shapes public opinion, laws, habits, and feelings, so democracy for him runs through daily life, not just the ballot box.
rationales.B: He describes a tendency toward equality, not a finished achievement.
rationales.C: This passage admires American democracy; it does not predict its failure.
rationales.D: Equality shapes the laws in his account; the laws do not create it.
rationales.general:
1. Follow his chain. Equality of conditions shapes opinion, then laws, then habits and feelings.
2. Notice the reach. He finds its influence beyond politics, in civil society itself.
3. Test the rivals. He never claims full equality, coming failure, or a constitutional cause.
Background: Tocqueville, a French aristocrat, came in 1831 to study prisons and wrote the classic account of American democracy.
Remember: when a visitor says a fact shapes everything, the claim is about culture, not only law.
